sections.title: Opening pages
sections.html:
A Note to the First Reader

This edition was created for one working Director of Nursing to react to honestly. It is not asking you to admire a finished product. It is asking a more useful question: does this sound like the job as it is actually lived?

The primary audience is a new, interim, newly promoted, or overwhelmed Director of Nursing in a Medicare- or Medicaid-certified long-term care facility. The federal framework is used as a common baseline. State requirements, facility policy, collective bargaining agreements, employment law, professional scope, and corporate directives may add obligations or change the correct response in a specific situation.

This is an educational leadership guide, not legal advice, clinical direction for an individual resident, or a guarantee of survey compliance. A DON must use current regulations, the facility's policies, the resident's plan of care, professional judgment, and appropriate consultation with the Administrator, medical director, infection preventionist, human resources, compliance, counsel, pharmacy, therapy, and other responsible leaders.

The regulatory source set for this first-reader edition was checked on August 27, 2026. CMS changes survey resources and interpretive guidance over time. Before using a tool operationally, compare it with the current CMS Nursing Homes page, current Appendix PP, the current Long-Term Care Survey Process procedure guide, and the applicable state survey agency guidance.

FIRST-READER REQUEST Mark anything that feels unrealistic, too generic, too idealized, or missing. The strongest version of this book should sound like an experienced DON is standing beside a new one at 6:40 a.m. on a difficult Monday - not like someone is describing the job from a conference room.

sections.title: Introduction - When Everything Becomes Yours
sections.html:
Introduction - When Everything Becomes Yours

At 6:12 a.m., before the first cup of coffee, the new DON already has seven messages. Night shift reports a fall with transfer to the emergency department. A nurse has called off. The wound consultant wants a decision. The staffing coordinator says two agency aides are on the schedule but one has not confirmed. The Administrator wants the morning numbers before the regional call. A family member has asked for a meeting. Someone has written "state is here" in a group text, then corrected it three minutes later: it was a vendor.

Nothing in the job description captures the feeling produced by those seven messages. The DON role is not difficult because it has one impossible task. It is difficult because many legitimate priorities arrive at the same time, each carried by a person who believes it should become the DON's first priority.

The new DON's first mistake is often to become the fastest responder in the building. Every question comes to the DON. Every fire is personally extinguished. Every schedule gap becomes a personal shift. Every report is rewritten. The building may feel calmer for a few days, but the system quietly learns a dangerous lesson: escalation is easier than ownership.

This four-week action plan takes a different approach. The DON's job is not to personally touch every task. The job is to make resident risk visible, clarify accountability, build reliable routines, intervene decisively when standards fail, and keep clinical leadership connected to the facility's operational decisions.

Federal survey rules reinforce that resident outcomes and the actual delivery of care matter more than a polished binder. The survey process uses observation, interview, record review, and professional judgment to assess whether the facility meets participation requirements. CMS's current Long-Term Care Survey Process also begins with offsite preparation and information available to the survey team before entry. The practical implication is simple: readiness is not a performance staged when surveyors enter. It is the daily condition of the care system. [1][2]

What the Four-Week Action Plan Promises

This action plan does not promise that four weeks will make the job easy. It promises something more credible: after four weeks, a DON should be able to answer seven questions with greater confidence.

What are the highest resident risks in this building today?

Which risks are controlled, and what evidence proves it?

Which staffing problems are symptoms of a deeper system problem?

Which leaders own which actions?

What does our QAPI work change at the bedside?

What does the Administrator need from nursing, and what does nursing need from the Administrator?

What must happen in the next 30, 60, and 90 days?

The Daily Rhythm

Each day contains one leadership objective, one field action, one conversation, and one piece of evidence. The sequence matters. Week One establishes visibility. Week Two establishes standards and staffing discipline. Week Three turns quality data into improvement work. Week Four aligns the DON with the Administrator, corporate leaders, and a sustainable first-90-day plan.

OPERATING PRINCIPLE Do not add a new meeting, spreadsheet, audit, or form unless it changes a decision, exposes a risk, assigns an owner, or verifies that an intervention worked.

Before Day One

☐ Obtain the current organizational chart and nursing leadership assignments.

☐ Obtain the most recent standard survey, complaint survey findings, Plans of Correction, and evidence of correction.

☐ Obtain the current facility assessment, QAPI plan, active PIP list, infection prevention risk assessment, emergency plan, and staffing plan.

☐ Obtain the last 90 days of incidents, hospital transfers, falls, pressure injuries, medication concerns, grievances, staffing hours, overtime, call-offs, agency use, and turnover information available to leadership.

☐ Schedule a protected weekly meeting with the Administrator.

☐ Identify who can answer questions about human resources, payroll-based staffing submissions, compliance, state reporting, and corporate policy.

sections.title: Week One - See the Building Before the Survey Does
sections.html:
Week One - See the Building Before the Survey Does

Survey readiness begins with disciplined curiosity. A new DON inherits stories about the building: "We always do it this way." "That tag was already fixed." "The family complains about everyone." "Night shift never documents." Some stories are accurate. Others are explanations repeated so often that no one tests them anymore.

Week One replaces inherited stories with visible evidence. The goal is not to conduct a miniature survey of every department. The goal is to establish a repeatable way to find risk, follow it to the resident, and verify that correction reaches practice.

WEEK ONE OUTCOME By Friday, the DON can name the building's five highest clinical or operational risks, show the evidence behind each one, identify the responsible leader, and describe the next verification step.

sections.title: Day 1 - Build the DON Command Center
sections.html:
Day 1 - Build the DON Command Center

Objective

Create one leadership view of the building that separates urgent resident risk from administrative noise.

Most new DONs inherit information in fragments: a wound list, an infection log, a falls binder, a staffing spreadsheet, text messages, handwritten notes, email flags, and a dashboard controlled by corporate staff. The problem is not always lack of information. It is the absence of one place where nursing leadership can see what requires action today.

The command center can be electronic or paper. It is not the medical record and must not become an unsecured repository of protected health information. It is a controlled leadership tool containing the minimum information necessary for follow-up.

Build Five Lanes

Immediate resident safety: new serious events, acute changes, allegations, elopement risk, significant medication issues, infection concerns, and urgent follow-up.

Time-sensitive clinical work: assessments, care-plan updates, provider notifications, treatment follow-up, dialysis or appointment coordination, labs, and high-risk transitions.

Staffing and capability: vacancies, call-offs, orientation gaps, competency concerns, overtime, agency coverage, and supervisor assignments.

Survey and compliance: open Plans of Correction, complaint or grievance follow-up, reportable events, audit failures, and expiring evidence.

Leadership commitments: Administrator requests, corporate deadlines, HR actions, QAPI owners, and decisions awaiting escalation.

The Three Labels

Every command-center item receives three labels: risk, owner, and next proof.

Risk answers: what can happen if this is not addressed?

Owner answers: who has authority to complete the next action?

Next proof answers: what will demonstrate completion or effectiveness?

"Check falls" is not a usable item. "Unit manager reviews the last three falls by 2 p.m. and reports whether interventions were implemented on the next shift" is usable because it names the work, owner, time, and verification.

Today's Field Action

☐ Collect the active lists currently used by nursing leadership.

☐ Eliminate duplicates that do not serve a distinct purpose.

☐ Select the five highest-risk items for today's leadership huddle.

☐ Assign an owner and next proof to each item.

☐ Set a fixed time to close the loop before leaving.

Conversation to Have

Ask each unit leader: "What are you worried could harm a resident or fail tonight if no one intervenes?" Then ask: "What evidence do you have, and what help do you need?"

Do not accept "everything" as an answer. A leader who cannot prioritize needs coaching in risk recognition, not a larger task list.

End-of-Day Evidence

The day is complete when every high-risk item has a named owner, a deadline, and a verification step. An item may remain open. It may not remain ownerless.

FAILURE MODE The DON becomes the owner of every item. If an action belongs to a unit manager, infection preventionist, staffing coordinator, MDS nurse, or another leader, keep ownership there and define the escalation point.

sections.title: Day 2 - Learn How Surveyors See the Building
sections.html:
Day 2 - Learn How Surveyors See the Building

Objective

Shift from department-centered readiness to resident-centered investigation.

Surveyors do not experience the building through the same categories used on the management meeting agenda. They may begin with offsite information, complaints, facility-reported incidents, staffing data, quality measures, and the facility's history. Inside the building, they observe, interview, and review records to determine whether care and services meet resident needs. [3][4]

This changes how a DON prepares. A clean nursing station does not resolve a concern if the resident, staff interview, care plan, treatment record, and observation tell different stories. The strongest readiness work follows the concern across those sources.

Practice the Four-Lens Review

Choose one current high-risk concern and examine it through four lenses.

Observation: What is happening now? Is equipment available? Are interventions actually in use? Does the resident appear comfortable, clean, safe, and treated with dignity?

Interview: What does the resident say? What does the direct-care employee understand? Do the nurse, unit manager, and family tell a consistent story?

Record: Do assessments, orders, care plans, progress notes, treatment records, and notifications support the care being delivered?

System: Was the issue recognized? Was risk analyzed? Were actions assigned? Did leadership verify effectiveness?

Use the Survey Resources as Mirrors

CMS publishes Critical Element Pathways and related survey resources. These are not checklists that guarantee compliance. They are valuable because they reveal the questions and evidence pathways surveyors may use. A DON can use the current pathway related to a concern to test whether the facility's practice, interviews, and records tell one coherent story.

Do not download an old pathway from an unverified training folder and assume it remains current. Use the CMS Nursing Homes survey-resource page and revision history.

Today's Field Action

☐ Select one resident with a current high-risk concern.

☐ Observe care before reading the entire chart.

☐ Speak with the resident when appropriate and with the direct-care employee.

☐ Review the relevant assessment, care plan, orders, implementation record, and follow-up.

☐ Record contradictions as system questions, not immediate accusations.

☐ Assign correction and a recheck time.

Conversation to Have

With the responsible nurse, ask: "Show me how the assessment became the care plan and how the care plan is reaching the resident on this shift."

This question is more revealing than "Is the chart complete?" It tests the path from recognition to action.

End-of-Day Evidence

Write a five-sentence tracer summary: concern, observation, interview, record, and next system action. If those sentences contradict one another, you have found useful work.

sections.title: Day 3 - Test Whether Past Corrections Still Hold
sections.html:
Day 3 - Test Whether Past Corrections Still Hold

Objective

Turn old deficiencies into current verification work.

A Plan of Correction can look complete while the correction has faded. Education occurred, an audit reached 100 percent for two weeks, and the binder was closed. Three months later a new employee is using the former process, the audit owner has transferred, or the intervention measures paper compliance instead of resident outcomes.

The new DON should not assume an old deficiency proves current failure. Nor should the DON assume an accepted Plan of Correction proves durable correction. Test it.

Read the Deficiency as a System Story

For each significant past deficiency, identify:

What happened to or could have happened to the resident?

What practice or system failed?

What scope was identified?

What immediate correction was promised?

How were other residents at risk identified?

What system change was promised?

Who was assigned monitoring, for how long, and where were results reported?

Then ask the question that is often skipped: what would prove this correction is still working today?

Test Durability

Choose a small current sample. Include different shifts, units, staff tenure, and resident conditions when relevant. Do not recreate a full survey unless the risk requires it. The purpose is to test whether the corrective system survived normal operations.

If it failed, avoid reflexively repeating the original education. Re-education is appropriate when knowledge is the cause. It is weak when the real cause is unclear ownership, inaccessible supplies, conflicting workflows, an unrealistic staffing assumption, or lack of supervisory follow-through.

Today's Field Action

☐ Select the two past deficiencies with the greatest potential resident impact.

☐ Locate the approved correction and monitoring plan.

☐ Sample current practice across more than one shift or unit when applicable.

☐ Compare the promised monitoring with the evidence actually retained.

☐ Reopen the action if the correction is no longer reliable.

☐ Place any recurring systemic concern on the QAPI risk list.

Conversation to Have

Ask the leader who owns the process: "If I did not show you the old Plan of Correction, how would you know today that this system is working?"

The answer should point to current practice and current evidence, not the existence of a binder.

End-of-Day Evidence

Complete one durability statement for each concern: "The correction appears sustained because..." or "The correction cannot yet be considered sustained because..."

COACHING POINT Treat a failed audit as information. Concealing or explaining away the result protects the old process. A clear failure gives leadership a chance to correct the system before another resident is harmed.

sections.title: Day 4 - Follow the Resident, Not the Binder
sections.html:
Day 4 - Follow the Resident, Not the Binder

Objective

Use resident-centered tracers to connect rights, assessment, care planning, implementation, and outcomes.

Federal requirements begin with the resident, including dignity, individuality, quality of life, and protection of rights. [5] A survey-ready clinical system must therefore do more than contain required documents. It must show that the facility recognized the resident's needs and preferences, planned appropriate care, delivered that care, monitored the result, and revised the approach when necessary.

Select the Right Tracers

Choose residents or situations that expose how the system performs under pressure. Examples include a recent admission, hospital return, new wound, repeated fall, weight change, behavior change, new psychotropic medication, dialysis coordination, anticoagulant use, infection concern, significant change, grievance, or discharge plan.

Avoid choosing only the cleanest chart. The purpose is learning, not self-congratulation.

Trace the Whole Path

For one resident, ask:

What matters to this resident, and how do we know?

What risks were recognized on admission and after changes?

Are orders, assessments, care-plan interventions, and assignment information aligned?

Can the employee providing care explain the interventions?

Is the intervention visible in practice?

Was the resident's response evaluated?

When the plan did not work, what changed?

Today's Field Action

☐ Complete two tracers in different clinical areas.

☐ Include at least one interview with a direct-care employee.

☐ Confirm that equipment and supplies are present and functional.

☐ Compare the resident's expressed preferences with the plan and observed care.

☐ Correct immediate safety issues through the appropriate clinical chain.

☐ Bring systemic findings to the next risk or QAPI review.

Conversation to Have

Ask the resident, when possible: "What do staff need to know to take good care of you today?" Then compare that answer with what the assigned caregiver says and what the plan directs.

End-of-Day Evidence

Document one example where the system worked and one gap that requires action. Read both at the next leadership huddle. Readiness grows when leaders study reliability, not only defects.

sections.title: Day 5 - Lead the First Hour of Survey
sections.html:
Day 5 - Lead the First Hour of Survey

Objective

Replace panic with a controlled, resident-centered response.

The first hour of survey should look like the building's normal leadership system becoming more visible, not a theatrical emergency. Staff should know whom to notify, how to welcome the team, where required information is maintained, how daily resident risk is managed, and how to answer questions truthfully.

Establish Roles Before Entry

Assign and rehearse these functions:

Entry lead: greets the survey team and follows the current entrance process.

Document coordinator: tracks requests, owners, time received, time due, and delivery.

Clinical response lead: coordinates resident-specific follow-up without disrupting care.

Rounding lead: verifies that normal standards continue throughout the building.

Communication lead: keeps the Administrator, corporate contacts, and department heads aligned.

These roles should match facility policy and current survey guidance. They should never be used to coach false answers, alter records, hide information, or interfere with surveyor access.

Teach the Staff Response

Employees do not need memorized speeches. They need permission to be truthful, concise, and resident-specific.

Listen to the entire question.

Answer what you know from your own role.

Demonstrate the normal process when asked.

Do not guess, argue, or create an answer.

If you do not understand the question, ask for clarification.

If you need to locate information, say so honestly.

Protect resident privacy while cooperating with the survey process.

Today's Field Action

☐ Verify the entrance and notification process.

☐ Confirm who owns each survey-response function.

☐ Locate the current survey resources and required facility information.

☐ Run a ten-minute document-request drill.

☐ Ask three employees how they would respond if a surveyor asked about a resident's care.

☐ Correct confusion without scripting a false or rehearsed answer.

Conversation to Have

Tell staff: "Survey readiness means showing the care you provide every day. If you do not know an answer, do not guess. Explain your role, find the right person, and keep the resident first."

End-of-Week Review

☐ We can name our five highest current risks.

☐ Every high-risk item has an owner and next proof.

☐ We have tested at least two past corrections for durability.

☐ We have completed resident-centered tracers across more than one clinical area.

☐ Survey-response roles are assigned and understood.

☐ We know which issues must move into QAPI or executive escalation.

sections.title: Week Two - Lead the Team You Actually Have
sections.html:
Week Two - Lead the Team You Actually Have

The staffing plan on paper is not the nursing team that reports tonight. The actual team includes strong employees carrying too much, new employees who still need supervision, reliable agency clinicians who know the residents, unfamiliar agency staff, burned-out supervisors, informal leaders, avoidant managers, and a few people whose behavior consumes attention far beyond their contribution.

A new DON does not have the luxury of waiting for the perfect team. The work is to make expectations visible, distinguish capability problems from conduct problems, act fairly, protect resident care, and build a staffing system that becomes less fragile over time.

WEEK TWO OUTCOME By Friday, the DON has defined three nonnegotiable nursing standards, addressed one avoided performance problem, mapped the causes of schedule instability, and launched a measured plan to reduce unnecessary agency dependence.

sections.title: Day 6 - Make Standards Visible
sections.html:
Day 6 - Make Standards Visible

Objective

Create a small number of observable nursing standards that apply across roles and shifts.

"Improve accountability" is not a standard. "The assigned nurse reviews new orders before the end of the shift and escalates any order that cannot be implemented" is a standard because people can observe it, teach it, and verify it.

When standards are vague, enforcement feels personal. One employee is corrected for behavior another employee is allowed to repeat. Supervisors improvise. Strong performers become resentful because reliability earns them more work while poor performance earns repeated rescue.

Choose Three Nonnegotiables

Start with standards linked to resident risk and daily reliability. Examples include:

Acute changes are assessed, communicated, documented, and followed through according to policy.

Assignments and high-risk interventions are understood before care begins.

Required treatments, medications, monitoring, and documentation are completed or escalated before shift end.

Do not launch ten priorities. Three consistently reinforced standards will reveal more than a long list nobody can remember.

Define Each Standard in Four Parts

Expected action: what must happen?

Time or trigger: when must it happen?

Evidence: how will a supervisor know?

Escalation: what happens when the standard cannot be met?

The fourth part matters. Employees sometimes hide unfinished work because leaders communicate that reporting a barrier is itself a failure. A safe system makes escalation an expectation while preserving accountability for preventable nonperformance.

Today's Field Action

☐ Select three high-risk, high-frequency nursing standards.

☐ Write each in observable language.

☐ Review them with unit managers and supervisors.

☐ Ask staff to explain the standards in their own words.

☐ Verify one standard on more than one shift.

☐ Correct inconsistent supervisory messages.

Conversation to Have

Tell the team: "A standard is not what we hope happens. It is what we teach, resource, observe, and address consistently. If a barrier prevents the standard, escalate it before the resident carries the risk."

End-of-Day Evidence

Each standard has a responsible supervisor, a verification method, and a clear escalation path.

sections.title: Day 7 - Handle the Difficult Employee Without Avoidance or Drama
sections.html:
Day 7 - Handle the Difficult Employee Without Avoidance or Drama

Objective

Address harmful conduct or unreliable performance through facts, expectations, and follow-through.

"Difficult" is a dangerous label because it can hide several different realities. One employee lacks skill. Another understands the work but refuses a reasonable expectation. Another reacts defensively because supervision has been inconsistent. Another raises a legitimate safety concern in an abrasive way. Another intimidates peers and undermines care.

The DON must identify the behavior, not diagnose the personality.

Prepare Before the Conversation

Separate four categories:

Fact: what was observed, documented, or reliably reported?

Impact: what resident, team, legal, or operational risk resulted?

Standard: what policy, job expectation, professional standard, or instruction applies?

Next action: what must change, by when, and how will it be verified?

Review the situation with human resources or the appropriate leader before taking formal action, especially when discipline, protected leave, disability accommodation, discrimination, retaliation, union rights, whistleblowing, resident allegations, licensure, or mandatory reporting may be involved.

Use a Calm Opening

"I want to discuss a specific concern from yesterday's shift. The treatment was not completed and was not escalated before shift change. That created a delay and left the oncoming nurse without a clear plan. Our expectation is that assigned treatments are completed or escalated before the end of the shift. Walk me through what happened."

Then listen. New facts may change the response. Listening does not erase the standard. It improves the accuracy of the decision.

Avoid the Two Traps

The first trap is arguing about attitude. Replace "your attitude is bad" with the observable behavior: interruption, refusal, raised voice, failure to follow direction, disrespectful statement, or incomplete work.

The second trap is making a threat the DON cannot or should not carry out. State the next step supported by policy and leadership authority. Do not promise termination, schedule changes, or board reporting without following the correct process.

Today's Field Action

☐ Select one performance or conduct concern that leadership has been avoiding.

☐ Verify the facts and applicable policy.

☐ Consult HR or the responsible leader when indicated.

☐ Conduct a private, respectful conversation.

☐ State the expectation, support available, deadline, and follow-up.

☐ Document according to policy.

End-of-Day Evidence

The employee can state what must change and when follow-up will occur. The supervisor can state what will be observed and documented.

LEADERSHIP TEST Fairness does not mean every employee receives the same intervention. It means decisions are based on relevant facts, policy, risk, prior coaching, role, and a consistent process rather than favoritism, frustration, or fear.

sections.title: Day 8 - Document Performance Fairly and Early
sections.html:
Day 8 - Document Performance Fairly and Early

Objective

Create performance documentation that supports improvement, protects fairness, and preserves an accurate leadership record.

Poor documentation often begins with good intentions. A supervisor gives repeated verbal reminders because the employee is short-staffed, likable, experienced, or going through a hard time. Months later, the behavior continues and the record makes it appear that no concern existed.

Documentation should not be saved only for the moment leadership wants to remove someone. It should be a normal part of coaching and accountability.

Write What Another Leader Can Understand

Strong documentation answers:

What occurred, and when?

What evidence supports the concern?

What standard or expectation applied?

What explanation did the employee provide?

What instruction, coaching, support, or action followed?

What improvement is expected?

When and how will follow-up occur?

Avoid loaded descriptions such as lazy, toxic, insubordinate, careless, or always negative unless a policy uses a defined term and the facts support it. Describe the action. "Employee left the medication cart unlocked and unattended in the hall for approximately four minutes" is useful. "Employee has no regard for safety" is a conclusion.

Document Improvement Too

If an employee corrects the behavior, record the improvement. Accountability should create a path back to reliability. A record that captures only failure teaches staff that leadership is building a case rather than leading performance.

Today's Field Action

☐ Review recent coaching notes for facts, standards, employee response, and follow-up.

☐ Correct vague language before it becomes the accepted record.

☐ Create a consistent supervisor coaching-note structure.

☐ Set follow-up dates for active concerns.

☐ Recognize documented improvement where it occurred.

Conversation to Have

Ask supervisors: "If another leader read this note six months from now, would that person understand what happened, what we expected, how the employee responded, and what we did next?"

End-of-Day Evidence

Every active performance concern has a documented next review date. No employee is left in indefinite informal coaching.

sections.title: Day 9 - Understand Why the Schedule Breaks
sections.html:
Day 9 - Understand Why the Schedule Breaks

Objective

Diagnose staffing instability before applying another incentive, agency request, or emergency schedule change.

Agency use is often treated as the problem. Sometimes it is the visible cost of deeper instability: vacancies, orientation failure, weekend inequity, inconsistent scheduling, delayed hiring, poor supervisor behavior, uncontrolled call-offs, avoidable turnover, census or acuity mismatch, or employees who reduce availability because the building feels unsafe.

Before reducing agency, identify what agency is currently protecting the facility from.

Map the Last 28 Days

Review the schedule by day, shift, unit, role, and source of coverage. Mark:

Open positions and time-to-fill

Call-offs and repeated patterns

Overtime and consecutive shifts

Agency hours and last-minute agency requests

Orientation shifts and new-hire loss

Leadership vacancies or supervisor coverage

Census and acuity changes

High-risk days that nearly failed

CMS requires facilities to submit auditable direct-care staffing information through the Payroll-Based Journal, including agency and contract staff. CMS uses staffing information with census data to report staffing levels, turnover, and tenure. [6] Even when a separate staffing office handles submission, the DON should understand what the data say about the operating reality.

Identify the Failure Type

Vacancy failure: authorized positions are not filled.

Availability failure: employees exist but are not available for required shifts.

Retention failure: new or existing employees leave faster than replacements stabilize.

Scheduling failure: available staff are deployed inefficiently or inequitably.

Capability failure: the scheduled number is present, but competencies do not match resident needs.

Leadership failure: supervisors do not support, communicate, or enforce consistently.

Demand failure: census or resident acuity exceeds the assumptions behind the staffing plan or facility assessment.

More than one type may be present. Each requires a different intervention.

Today's Field Action

☐ Map 28 days of coverage and instability.

☐ Identify the three shifts or units driving the greatest agency and overtime use.

☐ Compare staffing assumptions with current resident needs and the facility assessment.

☐ Ask recent hires and reliable employees what makes a shift workable or unworkable.

☐ Select one cause that can be changed within 14 days.

End-of-Day Evidence

Write a staffing diagnosis in one paragraph. It should explain why the schedule breaks, not merely report how many hours were uncovered.

sections.title: Day 10 - Reduce Agency Dependence Without Breaking the Building
sections.html:
Day 10 - Reduce Agency Dependence Without Breaking the Building

Objective

Reduce avoidable agency use through controlled replacement, retention, and schedule reliability while maintaining safe care.

An order to "eliminate agency by next month" can produce a cleaner budget line and a more dangerous building if internal capacity is not ready. The correct goal is not zero agency at any cost. The goal is a stable workforce with the right number, competencies, supervision, and continuity for resident needs, using outside coverage deliberately when it remains necessary.

Use a Four-Step Reduction Plan

Stabilize

Stop preventable daily failure. Confirm schedules earlier, strengthen weekend leadership, standardize call-off escalation, verify agency credentials and orientation, and prevent unplanned double shifts from becoming normal.

Convert

Identify reliable agency staff who may be interested in facility employment when lawful and consistent with vendor agreements. Improve hiring speed. Remove unnecessary delay between application, interview, offer, screening, orientation, and independent assignment.

Retain

Protect the people already carrying the building. Review schedule fairness, supervisor conduct, workload, orientation support, equipment access, recognition, and avoidable administrative friction. Do not rely only on bonuses.

Reduce in Steps

Target the agency hours that have a ready internal replacement. Reduce by shift or unit, verify resident care and overtime impact, then continue. A reduction that causes excessive overtime, turnover, missed care, or unsafe assignments is not sustainable.

Track the Balanced Scorecard

Do not celebrate agency reduction alone. Review agency hours together with vacancies, overtime, call-offs, turnover, orientation completion, staffing complaints, missed or delayed care, incidents, and leadership coverage.

Today's Field Action

☐ Establish the current four-week agency-hour baseline.

☐ Separate planned agency coverage from last-minute requests.

☐ Choose one shift or unit for a controlled reduction.

☐ Name the internal capacity that will replace those hours.

☐ Set resident-care and employee-impact guardrails.

☐ Review results weekly with the Administrator and staffing leader.

Conversation to Have

Tell the Administrator: "I support reducing avoidable agency use. I want us to track the replacement capacity and resident-care guardrails at the same time, so the savings reflect true stability rather than transferred risk."

End-of-Week Review

☐ Three nursing standards are visible and being verified.

☐ One avoided performance issue has been addressed through the correct process.

☐ Active coaching has documented follow-up dates.

☐ We can explain why our schedule breaks.

☐ Agency reduction is tied to real replacement capacity.

☐ Overtime, call-offs, turnover, competence, and resident outcomes are reviewed with agency hours.

sections.title: Week Three - Make QAPI Useful
sections.html:
Week Three - Make QAPI Useful

QAPI fails when it becomes a monthly recital of numbers. Falls are up. Weight loss is down. Agency is over budget. Education was completed. The meeting ends, but no one can explain which system is changing, who owns the test, or when leadership will know whether it worked.

Federal requirements describe QAPI as ongoing, comprehensive, data-driven, and focused on the full range of care and services. CMS organizes the framework around five elements: design and scope; governance and leadership; feedback, data systems, and monitoring; performance improvement projects; and systematic analysis and systemic action. [7][8]

Week Three converts those words into a simple operating discipline: choose a meaningful problem, understand the system, test a change, and verify the effect.

WEEK THREE OUTCOME By Friday, the DON has one defensible PIP charter, a small balanced measure set, a named executive sponsor and process owner, and a meeting rhythm that produces actions instead of minutes alone.

sections.title: Day 11 - Turn QAPI Into a Management System
sections.html:
Day 11 - Turn QAPI Into a Management System

Objective

Connect quality improvement to daily leadership decisions rather than a separate monthly committee ritual.

QAPI is not the DON's private project. The governing body is responsible and accountable for the QAPI program, and the program must include leadership, data, projects, analysis, and action across the facility. [7][9] The DON is often central to the work because many high-risk systems involve nursing, but central does not mean solely responsible.

Translate the Five Elements

Design and Scope

What care and service systems must the program cover? Does the QAPI plan reflect the actual resident population and the facility assessment, or does it repeat a generic corporate template?

Governance and Leadership

Who removes barriers, allocates resources, and holds leaders accountable? Which problems require Administrator, medical director, governing body, or corporate action rather than another nursing audit?

Feedback, Data Systems, and Monitoring

What information reveals performance? Include resident and family feedback, staff observations, incidents, complaints, audits, outcomes, staffing information, and other reliable sources.

Performance Improvement Projects

Which important problems receive focused, structured improvement work? A PIP should be chosen for significance, not because it is easiest to measure.

Systematic Analysis and Systemic Action

What process, environment, decision, resource, communication, or design factor allowed the problem? What change reaches the system rather than only the person closest to the event?

Today's Field Action

☐ Locate the current QAPI plan and committee structure.

☐ Identify where each of the five elements is visible in current practice.

☐ List important risks that are not represented in the QAPI agenda.

☐ Identify items that belong to routine management rather than a PIP.

☐ Confirm the Administrator and governing-body reporting path.

☐ Remove at least one report or agenda item that produces no decision or action.

Conversation to Have

Ask the Administrator: "Which quality risks would you be unable to explain confidently to the governing body today, and what information would change that?"

End-of-Day Evidence

The QAPI agenda can be traced to actual facility risks, and every agenda category has a defined decision purpose.

sections.title: Day 12 - Choose Measures That Reveal Risk
sections.html:
Day 12 - Choose Measures That Reveal Risk

Objective

Build a small measure set that helps leadership distinguish signal from noise.

Data can hide risk when leaders collect too much, use inconsistent definitions, or celebrate a rate without examining the resident experience behind it. A monthly number is useful only when the team knows what is included, who validates it, what comparison matters, and what decision follows.

Use a Balanced Measure

For a priority problem, select measures from four perspectives.

Outcome: what happened to residents? Examples include injury, hospitalization, pressure injury progression, infection, weight change, or successful discharge.

Process: was the intended care process completed reliably? Examples include timely assessment, intervention implementation, follow-up, reconciliation, or notification.

Balancing: did the improvement create another problem? Examples include overtime, restraints, emergency transfers, delayed medications, workload concentration, or new complaints.

Experience: what do residents, families, and staff report about the process?

Define Before You Trend

Write a measure definition that another leader could reproduce. Specify numerator, denominator when applicable, data source, owner, frequency, exclusions, validation method, and what level or pattern triggers review.

Do not move the definition whenever the result is uncomfortable. If a definition must change, document why and identify the break in the trend.

Today's Field Action

☐ Select one active quality risk.

☐ Choose one outcome, one process, and one balancing measure.

☐ Add an experience measure when the resident or staff perspective is important.

☐ Define the data source and owner.

☐ Validate a small sample against the underlying record.

☐ State the decision each measure is intended to support.

Conversation to Have

Ask the data owner: "If this number improves, what will we believe changed at the bedside? What other evidence would confirm it?"

End-of-Day Evidence

Every measure on the selected dashboard has a written definition and a decision rule.

DATA CAUTION A perfect audit can coexist with poor outcomes if the audit measures documentation rather than care, samples only convenient records, or allows the reviewer to correct the item while auditing it.

sections.title: Day 13 - Select a Performance Improvement Project
sections.html:
Day 13 - Select a Performance Improvement Project

Objective

Choose a PIP that is important enough to matter and focused enough to manage.

Not every defect requires a PIP. Some problems need immediate correction, routine supervision, policy clarification, equipment replacement, or a single accountable decision. A PIP is appropriate when the problem is significant, recurring, high-risk, complex, cross-functional, or resistant to ordinary correction.

Apply the Six-Question Test

Does the problem affect resident safety, rights, quality of care, or quality of life?

Is there evidence of a pattern, recurrence, or systemic vulnerability?

Does the problem cross departments, shifts, or workflows?

Is the current cause uncertain or oversimplified?

Can leadership influence the system within a useful time frame?

Will the project have an executive sponsor, process owner, team, and protected review rhythm?

If the answer to the last question is no, starting the PIP may create paperwork without improvement.

Write the Problem Without Writing the Solution

Weak problem statement: "Staff need more education about falls."

Stronger problem statement: "During the last eight weeks, six of nine repeat falls occurred during toileting or transfer periods on evening and night shifts. In five cases, the current transfer or toileting intervention was not consistently available to or followed by the assigned caregiver."

The stronger statement defines the pattern without assuming education is the cause.

Build the Charter

The charter should include:

Problem statement and resident impact

Current baseline

Aim with target and time frame

Scope and exclusions

Executive sponsor

Process owner and team

Measures

Initial analysis questions

First change test

Review schedule

Escalation needs

Today's Field Action

☐ Score candidate problems using the six-question test.

☐ Select one primary PIP rather than launching several weak projects.

☐ Write a fact-based problem statement.

☐ Confirm sponsor, owner, team, and meeting rhythm.

☐ Define a modest first test before designing a facility-wide rollout.

End-of-Day Evidence

The PIP charter names a problem, not a preferred solution, and leadership has agreed to support the work.

sections.title: Day 14 - Find the System Behind the Event
sections.html:
Day 14 - Find the System Behind the Event

Objective

Move beyond "staff failed to follow policy" to a defensible analysis of how the work system produced the event.

Individual accountability matters. It is also incomplete. If several competent people make similar errors in the same workflow, or if correct performance requires memory, workarounds, unavailable supplies, conflicting instructions, or unrealistic timing, the system is contributing.

System analysis does not excuse reckless or intentional behavior. It helps leadership decide whether the response should include individual action, system action, or both.

Build the Event Timeline

Use known facts to reconstruct what happened before, during, and after the event. Include handoffs, assignments, changes in condition, orders, alarms, equipment, staffing, interruptions, communication, supervision, and escalation.

Mark facts separately from assumptions. "The aide did not care" is an assumption. "The assignment sheet listed two different transfer methods" is a fact.

Ask Across Six System Domains

Person and competency: Was training, competency, fatigue, impairment, workload, or role clarity relevant?

Task and workflow: Was the process clear, usable, sequenced, and realistic?

Tools and environment: Were equipment, supplies, technology, space, and alarms available and functional?

Communication and information: Did the right person receive accurate, timely information?

Supervision and leadership: Was oversight present? Were prior warning signals addressed?

Organizational conditions: Did staffing, policy, incentives, resource limits, culture, or competing priorities shape the event?

Design Stronger Actions

Education is often necessary but rarely sufficient for a recurring system problem. Stronger actions may include simplifying the workflow, forcing a verification step, standardizing equipment placement, clarifying decision authority, changing assignment design, reducing handoff variation, adding direct observation, or removing a conflicting policy.

Today's Field Action

☐ Choose one recurring event or failed process.

☐ Build a fact-based timeline.

☐ Separate confirmed facts, missing information, and assumptions.

☐ Review all six system domains.

☐ Identify individual and system accountability separately.

☐ Select one small, measurable change test.

Conversation to Have

Ask the team: "What made the wrong action easier or more likely than the right action, and what would make the right action more reliable on the hardest shift?"

End-of-Day Evidence

The chosen intervention addresses at least one verified contributing factor. It is not merely a generic response attached to the event.

sections.title: Day 15 - Run a QAPI Meeting That Produces Action
sections.html:
Day 15 - Run a QAPI Meeting That Produces Action

Objective

Conduct a disciplined meeting that turns information into decisions, ownership, and verification.

A useful QAPI meeting does not read every dashboard cell aloud. Participants receive routine information in advance. Meeting time is reserved for variance, risk, decisions, barriers, learning, and action.

Use a Decision Agenda

Resident voice and urgent safety signals

Previous action closure and evidence of effectiveness

Measure exceptions and meaningful trends

PIP learning: what was tested, what happened, what changes next

New risks requiring prioritization

Resource or executive decisions

Owners, deadlines, and verification

Require Three Statements

For every reported concern, the presenter should be able to state:

What do we know?

What do we not yet know?

What decision or action is needed from this group?

This prevents the meeting from becoming an exchange of untested explanations.

Close the Loop

Minutes should preserve decisions and accountability, not transcribe conversation. Record the action, owner, due date, verification evidence, and escalation path. Begin the next meeting with incomplete actions and evidence of effectiveness.

Today's Field Action

☐ Send routine data before the meeting.

☐ Limit live review to exceptions and decisions.

☐ Confirm attendance by leaders with authority to act.

☐ Assign one owner for each action.

☐ State what evidence will close each action.

☐ Escalate resource barriers rather than carrying them as permanent nursing workarounds.

Conversation to Have

At the end of each issue, ask: "What will be different before the next meeting, who owns it, and what evidence will we review?"

End-of-Week Review

☐ Our QAPI plan reflects actual facility risk and the five CMS elements.

☐ Priority measures have definitions, owners, and decision rules.

☐ One PIP has a defensible charter and executive sponsor.

☐ The first change test addresses a verified contributing factor.

☐ Meeting actions have owners, due dates, and verification evidence.

☐ Resource barriers are visible to leaders with authority to resolve them.

sections.title: Week Four - Lead Up, Out, and Through
sections.html:
Week Four - Lead Up, Out, and Through

Many DONs are evaluated on results they cannot produce alone. Nursing may be accountable for clinical systems while staffing decisions, capital purchases, admissions, payroll, HR timelines, vendor contracts, and corporate targets are controlled elsewhere. The DON who quietly absorbs every gap becomes indispensable for the wrong reason: the organization stops seeing the cost of unresolved system problems.

Week Four builds the leadership relationships and boundaries that allow nursing to influence those decisions without retreating into conflict or silent overfunctioning.

WEEK FOUR OUTCOME By Friday, the DON and Administrator have a working compact, corporate requests are translated into safe operational plans, the first 90 days have measurable priorities, and the DON has a sustainable escalation and boundary system.

sections.title: Day 16 - Build the DON-Administrator Compact
sections.html:
Day 16 - Build the DON-Administrator Compact

Objective

Create a clear operating agreement between the facility's two most interdependent leaders.

The DON and Administrator do not need identical perspectives. The Administrator holds broad responsibility for facility management and accountability to the governing body. The DON holds nursing leadership responsibilities shaped by professional standards, regulation, resident needs, facility policy, and the organization's structure. [10] Productive tension can protect the facility when both leaders bring the full picture to decisions.

Unproductive tension emerges when expectations remain implied. The Administrator assumes the DON will cover a staffing gap. The DON assumes the Administrator understands the clinical risk of an admission decision. Corporate assumes an audit score proves implementation. Each person acts on a different mental model.

Agree on Six Things

Daily risk communication: what must be reported immediately, by whom, and through what channel?

Decision rights: which decisions belong to nursing, the Administrator, a joint review, or corporate approval?

Staffing escalation: what conditions trigger executive action, admission limits, contract coverage, or another response?

Survey and incident response: who coordinates reports, notifications, communication, and evidence?

Resource decisions: how are equipment, vendor, recruitment, education, and overtime needs evaluated?

Conflict repair: how will the leaders handle disagreement without undermining one another in front of staff?

Use a Weekly One-on-One

Protect a 30-minute weekly meeting with a standing agenda. Discuss the top risks, staffing stability, survey or compliance actions, QAPI decisions, resident or family escalation, people decisions, corporate deliverables, and commitments from the prior week.

Do not use the entire meeting to replay daily events. Use it for decisions the two leaders must own together.

Today's Field Action

☐ Schedule or reset the weekly Administrator-DON meeting.

☐ Agree on immediate, daily, and weekly communication categories.

☐ Clarify three recurring decision-right conflicts.

☐ Define staffing escalation thresholds.

☐ Agree on how disagreements will be repaired.

☐ Record joint commitments and review them next week.

Conversation to Have

"I want us to be able to disagree early and privately, then give the building a clear decision. What information do you need from me to make that possible, and what decisions do I need from you?"

End-of-Day Evidence

Both leaders can state the top three joint risks and the next decision each one owns.

sections.title: Day 17 - Make Corporate Expectations Work Safely
sections.html:
Day 17 - Make Corporate Expectations Work Safely

Objective

Convert targets, deadlines, and directives into executable plans with visible assumptions and risks.

Corporate expectations may be clinically appropriate and operationally difficult at the same time. Reduce agency. Improve admissions. Lower overtime. Complete education. Eliminate audit variance. Increase census. Close Plans of Correction. Each target becomes safer when the DON translates it into capacity, sequence, ownership, and guardrails.

Use the Translation Questions

For every significant directive, ask:

What outcome is corporate seeking?

What deadline and measurement definition apply?

What current baseline and capacity assumptions are being used?

What work must occur at the facility level?

Which departments and resources are required?

What resident-care, staffing, compliance, or retention risks could the plan create?

What guardrails and escalation points are necessary?

What evidence will demonstrate progress and effectiveness?

The goal is not to reject pressure. It is to turn pressure into a plan that can be owned and monitored.

Escalate With Options

Weak escalation: "We cannot do this."

Stronger escalation: "We can reduce these agency hours by the target date if two open nurse positions are filled and weekend call-offs remain below the defined threshold. Without that replacement capacity, the available options are continued agency use, increased overtime, or adjusted admissions. My recommendation is the staged reduction attached, with weekly resident-care and workforce guardrails."

The stronger version names assumptions, alternatives, and a recommendation.

Today's Field Action

☐ Select one current corporate target creating pressure.

☐ Write the baseline, required outcome, deadline, and assumptions.

☐ Identify dependencies outside nursing.

☐ State the resident and workforce guardrails.

☐ Present options and a recommendation.

☐ Document the decision and review date.

End-of-Day Evidence

The target has an executable facility plan, visible dependencies, and an agreed escalation point.

sections.title: Day 18 - Design the First 90 Days
sections.html:
Day 18 - Design the First 90 Days

Objective

Sequence leadership work so urgent problems are controlled without abandoning long-term stabilization.

The first 90 days should not be a list of everything the DON wants to improve. It should explain what must be stabilized first, what systems will be built next, and what progress can reasonably be demonstrated by Day 90.

Days 1-30: Stabilize and See

Priorities include immediate resident safety, reportable-event reliability, high-risk clinical systems, staffing coverage, leadership roles, open survey actions, and the daily risk rhythm. The DON listens widely but does not postpone action on clear safety concerns.

Evidence may include a working risk huddle, assigned owners, verified corrections, leadership rounding, a staffing diagnosis, and an agreed Administrator communication rhythm.

Days 31-60: Standardize and Strengthen

Priorities include visible nursing standards, supervisor capability, orientation, performance follow-up, schedule reliability, targeted agency reduction, and one focused PIP.

Evidence may include consistent verification across shifts, completed competency actions, improved schedule confirmation, reduced last-minute agency requests, a functioning PIP charter, and closed leadership commitments.

Days 61-90: Sustain and Prove

Priorities include durability checks, trend review, QAPI effectiveness, succession or backup coverage, policy-workflow alignment, and executive reporting.

Evidence may include sustained practice across a fresh sample, balanced outcome measures, a reduced backlog, improved staffing stability, and a governing-body or corporate report that connects actions to resident care.

Limit the Plan

Choose no more than five enterprise priorities for the first 90 days. Routine operations continue, but the priority list defines the systems receiving concentrated leadership attention.

Today's Field Action

☐ Write five or fewer 90-day priorities.

☐ Place each priority in stabilize, standardize, or sustain.

☐ Define one or two measures of progress for each.

☐ Name dependencies and executive decisions.

☐ Identify what will not be attempted during this period.

☐ Review the plan with the Administrator and nursing leaders.

End-of-Day Evidence

The plan can fit on one page and allows another leader to understand what success means by Days 30, 60, and 90.

Phase

Priority work

Evidence by phase end

Executive needs

Days 1-30

Stabilize and see

Risks, owners, staffing diagnosis, survey actions

Decisions and immediate resources

Days 31-60

Standardize and strengthen

Reliable standards, supervisor follow-up, active PIP

Cross-functional support

Days 61-90

Sustain and prove

Durability, balanced trends, executive report

Longer-term investment

sections.title: Day 19 - Protect Clinical Judgment and Professional Boundaries
sections.html:
Day 19 - Protect Clinical Judgment and Professional Boundaries

Objective

Recognize when leadership pressure requires clarification, escalation, documentation, delegation, or refusal through the proper channel.

The DON role carries moral and professional pressure. A DON may be asked to accept an admission when staffing or capability feels inadequate, cover another shift after repeated excessive hours, sign an audit not personally verified, delay an escalation to avoid attention, or take responsibility for a system controlled by another department.

The correct response depends on facts, urgency, resident risk, professional obligations, state law, policy, and authority. A book cannot decide those cases. It can provide a disciplined sequence.

Use the Boundary Sequence

Clarify the request. What exactly is being asked, by whom, and by when?

Identify the risk. What resident, legal, ethical, licensure, staffing, or operational concern exists?

Verify the governing source. Review current policy, regulation, professional standard, contract, or legal guidance as appropriate.

State the concern factually. Avoid emotional escalation or unsupported conclusions.

Offer a safe alternative when one exists.

Escalate through the defined chain.

Document the request, facts, concerns, advice received, decision, and actions according to policy.

Act immediately when resident protection or mandatory reporting requires it.

Distinguish Support From Substitution

Helping a supervisor through a difficult event is leadership. Permanently completing that supervisor's work is substitution. Covering an unexpected emergency shift may be necessary. Becoming the unplanned staffing model is not sustainable.

Boundaries become credible when the DON also delegates clearly, follows through, and meets legitimate commitments. A leader who says no to everything will not be trusted when the risk is real. A leader who says yes to everything will eventually be unable to protect anything.

Today's Field Action

☐ Identify one recurring request that transfers unmanaged risk to the DON.

☐ Clarify the decision right and escalation path.

☐ State the concern using facts and resident impact.

☐ Propose a safe alternative or required resource.

☐ Document the final decision as appropriate.

☐ Identify backup leadership so the DON is not the only safe escalation point.

End-of-Day Evidence

At least one recurring risk has moved from private burden to visible organizational decision.

sections.title: Day 20 - Build a Leadership System You Can Sustain
sections.html:
Day 20 - Build a Leadership System You Can Sustain

Objective

Create a personal operating system that protects follow-through, judgment, and endurance.

The DON cannot control when every incident, absence, complaint, survey, or corporate request arrives. The DON can control how priorities are captured, how work is delegated, when decisions are reviewed, and how unfinished risk is escalated.

Keep Four Leadership Rhythms

Daily

Clinical risk huddle, staffing review, high-risk resident follow-up, leadership rounding, and end-of-day closure of urgent commitments.

Weekly

Administrator-DON meeting, staffing stability review, active performance follow-up, survey or compliance action review, and PIP progress.

Monthly

QAPI decision meeting, trend analysis, competency and education review, agency and overtime analysis, policy or workflow priorities, and executive reporting.

Quarterly

Facility assessment review as required by regulation and when significant changes occur, deeper workforce review, emergency readiness, succession and backup planning, program effectiveness, and 90-day priority reset. Always follow the current regulatory frequency and triggers rather than a generic calendar alone.

Protect Decision Quality

Fatigue narrows thinking and increases reactivity. The solution is not a wellness slogan placed on top of an impossible workload. It is a leadership system that names backup coverage, limits unnecessary after-hours escalation, distributes authority, closes recurring failure loops, and makes resource gaps visible.

The DON should know:

Which events require immediate personal notification

Which events can follow the normal supervisor chain

Who acts when the DON is unavailable

Which decisions require Administrator or corporate involvement

How unresolved risk is documented and handed off

When workload itself has become a safety or professional-practice concern requiring escalation

Today's Field Action

☐ Put the four leadership rhythms on the calendar.

☐ Define immediate and next-business-day escalation categories.

☐ Name and prepare backup leaders.

☐ Remove one recurring report or meeting that creates no action.

☐ Select the five priorities for the next 30 days.

☐ Schedule a Day-30 review with the Administrator.

The Final Question

The most useful test of a DON's leadership is not whether the building can survive a heroic week. It is whether the building becomes more reliable without requiring heroics as its normal operating method.

End-of-Week Review

☐ The DON and Administrator have a functioning weekly compact.

☐ Corporate targets are translated into plans with assumptions and guardrails.

☐ The 30-60-90 day plan has five or fewer priorities.

☐ Professional and operational boundaries have defined escalation paths.

☐ Backup leaders know their authority.

☐ The daily, weekly, monthly, and quarterly rhythms are scheduled.

The assessment must address the resident population, resources, staffing competencies, and participation by facility leadership, including the Director of Nursing. https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/chapter-IV/subchapter-G/part-483/subpart-B/section-483.71

sections.title: Field Tools
sections.html:
Field Tools

These tools are designed to support decisions and verification. They should be adapted to the facility's current policies, systems, privacy practices, and state requirements. Do not duplicate protected health information into an unsecured workbook.

Tool 1 - The 15-Minute Clinical Risk Huddle

Purpose

Create a brief daily view of resident risk, staffing capability, and actions requiring leadership coordination.

Participants

DON or designee, unit leaders, staffing or scheduling representative, MDS or care-management representative as useful, infection prevention or other clinical leaders based on facility structure. The Administrator joins or receives the escalated decisions according to the facility's operating rhythm.

Agenda

New serious events, allegations, acute changes, transfers, infections, and urgent follow-up

High-risk residents whose interventions changed or failed

Staffing gaps, competency concerns, and leadership coverage

Time-sensitive assessments, treatments, labs, appointments, or transitions

Survey, complaint, Plan of Correction, grievance, or reporting actions

Owners, deadlines, and next proof

Huddle Rules

Protect privacy and use the minimum necessary information.

Do not solve every issue in the huddle.

Assign one owner for the next action.

Name the escalation point.

Close yesterday's high-risk actions before adding routine new work.

Today's Huddle Record

Priority risk:

Owner and deadline:

Next proof:

Executive decision needed:

sections.title: Tool 2 - Survey-Readiness Rounding Guide
sections.html:
Tool 2 - Survey-Readiness Rounding Guide

Resident Experience

☐ Resident is treated with dignity, privacy, and respect.

☐ Resident can explain how to request help and reports that needs are addressed.

☐ Preferences visible in conversation are reflected in care.

☐ Call system, mobility aids, protective equipment, and personal items are accessible as appropriate.

Care Delivery

☐ Current assignment information reflects high-risk interventions.

☐ Assigned staff can explain resident-specific care.

☐ Orders, assessments, care plan, implementation, and observed care align.

☐ Treatments, monitoring, and follow-up are complete or appropriately escalated.

sections.title: A Closing Note to the DON
sections.html:
A Closing Note to the DON

The DON role places one person at the meeting point of resident vulnerability, workforce reality, regulatory scrutiny, family expectations, clinical judgment, and financial pressure. That position can create deep purpose. It can also create the false belief that a strong DON should be able to absorb unlimited responsibility without showing strain.

Strength in this role is not silent endurance. It is the ability to see risk clearly, tell the truth about capacity, develop other leaders, correct behavior fairly, demand evidence, escalate decisions to the right level, and protect the resident when pressure makes compromise feel convenient.

There will still be difficult mornings. A four-week action plan cannot remove them. It can help a DON enter those mornings with a system: the highest risk is visible, the next action has an owner, the Administrator knows what decision is needed, the team knows the standard, and unfinished work has an honest path forward.

That is not perfect control. It is credible leadership.

sections.title: About This First-Reader Edition
sections.html:
About This First-Reader Edition

The New DON's First 90 Days is structured as a four-week action plan for new, interim, and overwhelmed Directors of Nursing in long-term care. It combines daily leadership actions, survey-readiness thinking, workforce stabilization, practical QAPI, executive alignment, and ready-to-use field tools that support the full first 90 days.

Written by Averose Pastores. This first-reader edition is a concept and reader-experience test. A future edition should be revised with direct input from experienced DONs, Administrators, long-term care clinicians, compliance leaders, and appropriate state-specific reviewers.
